title: "Tea basics"

{{< include _includes/lang-switcher/tea-basics.en.qmd >}}


You have a mug, hot water, and a small pile of dry leaves—or a paper bag from the grocery aisle. Pour the water on. Wait a few minutes. The water changes color and the room smells different. That drink is what people usually mean by **tea**.

In the same aisle you will also find boxes labeled "tea" that are made from other plants—chamomile, peppermint, or rooibos, for example. Those drinks can be pleasant, but they are not the same as tea made from the tea plant. This page starts with that everyday distinction: what is in the mug, how to make one simple cup, and a few names you are likely to see. Longer shelf lists live on [Tea labels](tea-labels.qmd). The later chapters go deeper into chemistry, body, history, and choice.

This page is meant as a gentle first step. It is not a name encyclopedia and not a chemistry lesson. Typical milligrams live on the [Cup reference](cup-reference.qmd). If a mug turns out bitter or flat, try [Kitchen troubleshoot](tea-troubleshoot.qmd).

Tap a footnote number to jump to the source, then the caret to jump back. Hover often shows a popup. A few short side-notes sit in collapsed **"More detail…"** foldouts.

::: {.callout-tip title="5-minute path"}
1. **True tea vs herbal** — tea-plant leaf, or another plant in hot water.
2. **Same plant, two paths** — heat the leaf early (green) or let it brown in air (black).
3. **Make one simple mug** — about 2 g of leaf in about 250 mL of hot water. Taste it. Do not memorize a chart.
4. **One feeling sentence** — tea-plant tea usually brings caffeine and L-theanine. Amounts vary → [Cup reference](cup-reference.qmd).
5. **More box names** — open [Tea labels](tea-labels.qmd).
6. **Ready for why?** — open [Chapter 1](modules/module-01/index.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Words to know on this page"}
- **True tea** — a drink from the tea plant (green, black, and the styles between them).
- **Herbal "tea" / tisane** — hot water on another plant (chamomile, peppermint, rooibos…).
- **Steep** — letting the leaf sit in hot water so the drink takes on color and taste.
:::

---

## True tea vs other plants in the mug

In everyday English, "tea" can mean almost anything steeped in hot water. That loose use is fine at a cafe counter. On this site, **true tea** means leaf—and sometimes the bud—of one plant: the tea plant ([*Camellia sinensis*](glossary.qmd#sinensis) in the glossary).

Many herbal boxes still say "tea" on the front. Chamomile, peppermint, ginger, and rooibos are usually infusions of **other plants**. They can be lovely. They are not the same drink as tea-plant green or black, and they are not the chemical story the later chapters tell. FDA consumer materials have long noted that herbal teas come from other plants and should name the plant on the label.[^1] Trade groups likewise ask shoppers to keep "tea" for tea-plant styles (green, black, oolong, white, dark) and call the rest herbals or tisanes.[^2]

So when a later chapter talks about what is in your mug, it assumes a tea-plant leaf unless it says otherwise. A caffeine-free "bedtime tea" made of chamomile is a different drink. Named herbal rows live on [Tea labels](tea-labels.qmd).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: why the word 'tea' got stretched"}
English borrowed the word *tea* for the tea-plant drink, then stretched it to any hot infusion. That stretch is fine at a cafe counter. It becomes confusing here, because the wake-up and calm-focus story belongs to the tea plant—not to every box that says "tea."
:::

---

## Same plant, different paths

Green and black tea usually come from the same plant. What changes is the **factory path**—how the leaf is handled after harvest—not which species sits on the shelf. The UK Tea & Infusions Association puts the split simply: how long oxidation runs during processing—or whether it runs at all—is what separates black, green, oolong, and white character.[^3]

| Path | Plain idea | What you usually notice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Green** | Heat the leaf early so it does not brown | Pale to yellow-green; grassy or vegetal |
| **Black** | Let the leaf brown in air, then dry | Amber to deep red-brown; malty or brisk |
| **In between, lighter, or aged** | Oolong sits between green and black; white is lighter handling; dark teas such as Pu-erh are aged | Still the same plant—different stopping points |

Tea makers often say "fermentation" for the green-to-black change. For ordinary green, oolong, and black tea they usually mean leaf enzymes plus air. True microbial aging shows up mainly in dark teas such as Pu-erh.[^4]

Bag versus loose leaf, and the black-tea factory words *orthodox* and *CTC*, are about **particle size**—not a new plant. Smaller pieces often color the mug faster. The grade table lives on [Tea labels](tea-labels.qmd).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: six type-names"}
Trade lists sometimes name **six** manufactured types (green, yellow, white, oolong, black, dark). Yellow tea is rare outside China. You do not need it before Chapter 1.[^5]

Oolong is a **range**, not one midpoint—so one cafe oolong can taste almost green and another almost black. Still one plant.
:::

---

## Your first mug

A simple home cup on this site is about **2 g** of dry leaf—one bag, or a modest spoon—in about **250 mL** of hot water. That is the everyday baseline the [Cup reference](cup-reference.qmd) uses when it talks about milligrams.[^6]

- **Black** tea is often made with water near boiling, for a few minutes.
- **Green** tea is often happier a little cooler, and a little shorter.

Taste the cup. If it is harsh, stop sooner next time. You do not need a chart in your head.

If something is off—bitter or flat—try [Kitchen troubleshoot](tea-troubleshoot.qmd). If you want to know why heat and time matter, open [Chapter 1 · Section 3](modules/module-01/03-brewing.qmd). Gear with a name (teapot, gaiwan, whisk) is listed on [Tea labels](tea-labels.qmd). Milligrams live on the [Cup reference](cup-reference.qmd).

---

## Awake, and a little calm

Tea-plant tea usually brings **caffeine** (the familiar wake-up) and **[L-theanine](glossary.qmd#l-theanine)** (a calm-focus amino acid in the leaf). How much of each depends on the leaf and the steep. This page does not give a dose and does not tell you what to drink for health.

Numbers live on the [Cup reference](cup-reference.qmd). The "three guests in the mug" story lives in [Chapter 1 · Section 4](modules/module-01/04-compounds.qmd).

---

## Three labels to recognize

Only three names here, on purpose. The long sheet is the next door.

| Name | Usual meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **English Breakfast** | Usually a strong **black blend**. Recipes vary by brand. |
| **Sencha** | Everyday Japanese **green**. |
| **Chamomile "tea"** | Usually **herbal** — another plant, not the tea plant. |

English Breakfast as a black blend, and green versus black as processing, follow the UK Tea & Infusions Association type pages already cited.[^3] Chamomile as another plant follows the FDA note above.[^1]

Chinese, Japanese, and Western cafe lists—grades, herbals, and teapot names included—are on [Tea labels](tea-labels.qmd).

[^1]: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. (1996). Tea: A story of serendipity. *FDA Consumer*. https://permanent.access.gpo.gov/lps1609/www.fda.gov/fdac/features/296_tea.html (Herbal teas are made from other plants and should name the plant.)

[^2]: Tea Association of the USA. (2019). Comment on FDA food standards of identity modernization (Docket FDA-2018-N-2381): true tea from *Camellia sinensis* (green, black, oolong, white, dark) vs herbal tisanes. https://downloads.regulations.gov/FDA-2018-N-2381-1376/attachment_1.pdf

[^3]: UK Tea & Infusions Association. Types of tea, origins & varieties. https://www.tea.co.uk/types-of-tea (Oxidation—or its absence—separates black, green, oolong, and white; English Breakfast as a black-tea blend.)

[^4]: Ordinary oolong/black "fermentation" is enzymatic oxidation; true microbial fermentation mainly in post-fermented teas such as Pu-erh. See Subramanian et al. (1999) and Tanaka & Kouno (2003) as cited in [Chapter 1](modules/module-01/index.qmd).

[^5]: Processing overviews commonly list six manufactured types (green, yellow, white, oolong, black, dark)—e.g. the tea-processing chapter in *Food Reviews International* (https://doi.org/10.1080/87559129509541052) and ISO tea-type classification work (ISO 20715:2023).

[^6]: Everyday baseline on the [Cup reference](cup-reference.qmd): about 2 g dry leaf per 250 mL. Formal tasting strength under ISO 3103:2019 is stronger (about 2 g per 100 mL)—https://www.iso.org/standard/73224.html—and that comparison stays on the Cup page.
